item.title: Cabinet to deliberate on CRC report before it goes to Parliament
item.description: The Constitutional Review Commission’s final report and proposed 2026 Draft Constitution will now go before Cabinet for consideration, following its formal submission to the President today. CRC Chairperson Sevuloni Ratumaiyale Valenitabua presented the Commission’s Review Report on the 2013 Constitution, together with the Draft Constitution of the Republic of Fiji 2026, to President Ratu Naiqama
item.content:encoded:
The Constitutional Review Commission’s final report and proposed 2026 Draft Constitution will now go before Cabinet for consideration, following its formal submission to the President today.

CRC Chairperson Sevuloni Ratumaiyale Valenitabua presented the Commission’s Review Report on the 2013 Constitution, together with the Draft Constitution of the Republic of Fiji 2026, to President Ratu Naiqama Lalabalavu at State House.

The President subsequently presented a copy of the report to Prime Minister Sitiveni Rabuka.

The Prime Minister is expected to table the report in Cabinet, where its recommendations will be deliberated before the document proceeds to Parliament through the appropriate constitutional and Government processes.

Acting Attorney-General Siromi Turaga stressed that the submission of the report does not mean the Government has adopted or approved any of the Commission’s recommendations.

“The Report represents the independent work of the Constitutional Review Commission following an extensive nationwide consultation process. It must now go through the appropriate Government processes before any further decisions are made,” Mr Turaga said.

He also confirmed that the report will not be released publicly at this stage.

It will be made available to the public in due course, following Cabinet deliberation and completion of the required processes.

Mr Turaga said the submission marked the completion of the CRC’s mandate and acknowledged the work of the Commissioners and staff involved in the review.

He also recognised the contribution of constitutional and legislative experts Professor Anthony Regan, Dr Kathrene Le Roy and Fiona Leonard.

Mr Turaga urged the public and stakeholders not to speculate on the contents of the report or its possible outcomes before it has been properly considered.

The report follows months of nationwide consultations by the CRC as part of the review of Fiji’s 2013 Constitution.

item.title: Hydro output under threat | EFL warns weather impact
item.description: A FORECAST of a severe El Niño could reduce rainfall and hydropower generation, forcing Energy Fiji Ltd (EFL) to rely more heavily on fuel-powered generation to keep electricity flowing. EFL chairman Rokoseru Nabalarua said the situation required careful management of the company’s generation mix as hydrology conditions deteriorated.
item.content:encoded:
A FORECAST of a severe El Niño could reduce rainfall and hydropower generation, forcing Energy Fiji Ltd (EFL) to rely more heavily on fuel-powered generation to keep electricity flowing.

EFL chairman Rokoseru Nabalarua said the situation required careful management of the company’s generation mix as hydrology conditions deteriorated.

Speaking at the Fiji Australia Business Council forum in Suva, Mr Nabalarua said the Monasavu hydro dam level had fallen to about 734 metres as of August 3, 2026, with rainfall forecast to remain below levels recorded in previous years.

“This will be one of the worst El Niño that the world will ever see for a long time,” Mr Nabalarua said.

“EFL is working with weather authorities, once every month, to plan for the expected conditions.”

The lower water levels mean EFL must balance hydropower with fossil-fuel generation to maintain electricity supply and avoid major disruptions.

Mr Nabalarua said the situation also highlighted the link between Fiji’s water resources and fuel costs.

“When hydro output is constrained, thermal dispatch, fuel usage and cost pressure increase.”

He said increased reliance on thermal generation could put pressure on EFL’s margins if fuel-related costs, including duties, surcharges and operating expenses, were not properly recovered.

Mr Nabalarua also acknowledged the Government’s duty-free concession for EFL during the current period, saying it would help protect the company’s financial position.

He said maintaining EFL’s financial strength was important to its long-term commercial viability.

However, Mr Nabalarua stressed that the surcharge mechanism was not a long-term solution to Fiji’s exposure to fossil fuels.

“The surcharge is not a substitute for transition.”

He said it was a temporary stabilising measure while EFL maintained reliable electricity supply, accelerated investment and worked to reduce its future reliance on fuel.

item.title: Court draws line on hospital upfront payments
item.description: PATIENTS requiring urgent medical treatment at Fiji’s public hospitals cannot be required to make upfront payments or provide guarantees of payment before receiving treatment because they cannot afford the money or are poor, the Supreme Court has ruled in a landmark judgement. The court has ruled in favour of a family whose relative was denied dialysis treatment because he could not pay.
item.content:encoded:
PATIENTS requiring urgent medical treatment at Fiji’s public hospitals cannot be required to make upfront payments or provide guarantees of payment before receiving treatment because they cannot afford the money or are poor, the Supreme Court has ruled in a landmark judgement.

The court has ruled in favour of a family whose relative was denied dialysis treatment because he could not pay.

The August 28 judgment was delivered by Justice Terence Arnold, with Justice Lowell Goddard and Justice Geoffrey Nettle agreeing with his reasoning and orders.

The case was brought by Rajesh Chandra, administrator of the estate of his late son, against the permanent secretary for Health, Ministry of Health and attorney-general.

Mr Chandra’s son suffered from chronic kidney disease and was admitted to Lautoka Hospital in June 2011. The court heard that while dialysis was available, the hospital would not provide it unless payment was made.

Justice Arnold said the Public Hospitals and Dispensaries Act, properly interpreted, did not allow hospitals to require payment before treating patients admitted because of urgency or poverty.

“Persons admitted under either category cannot be required to make an upfront payment, or to give a guarantee of payment, for their treatment,” Justice Arnold said.

He found Mr Chandra’s son fell within the category of a person needing prompt treatment and said there was no statutory basis for withholding short-term dialysis because he could not afford it.

“This was not only a breach of the PHD Act – it was a failure by the medical staff involved to meet the duty of care which the common law places upon them,” Justice Arnold said.

Justice Arnold concluded that the medical staff were negligent in failing to provide necessary treatment on a lawful basis.

The Supreme Court granted leave to appeal, allowed the appeal and set aside the decisions of both the Court of Appeal and High Court.

The matter has been remitted to the High Court for assessment of damages.

The permanent secretary for Health, the Ministry of Health and the attorney-general were ordered to pay $20,000 in costs for the High Court proceedings, $15,000 for the Court of Appeal and $15,000 for the Supreme Court proceedings.

item.title: Airline’s fuel costs soar
item.description: FIJI Airways’ fuel bill increased by $130 million in the first half of 2026 compared with the same period last year, with the airline warning the additional cost could reach up to $300m for the full year. Fiji Airways chief executive officer Paul Scurrah said the sharp increase in fuel costs was making trading conditions difficult for airlines worldwide.
item.content:encoded:
FIJI Airways’ fuel bill increased by $130 million in the first half of 2026 compared with the same period last year, with the airline warning the additional cost could reach up to $300m for the full year.

Fiji Airways chief executive officer Paul Scurrah said the sharp increase in fuel costs was making trading conditions difficult for airlines worldwide.

Mr Scurrah attributed the increase to the conflict in the Middle East, describing it as the worst fuel shock in 50 years.

“The higher fuel costs has prompted many airlines to reduce the amount of flying they operated,” he said.

However, he said Fiji Airways had chosen to maintain its overall level of flying while making changes to its network.

“Whilst most of the industry is retreating, we are doing the opposite.”

Mr Scurrah said the airline had withdrawn from some routes while introducing additional services elsewhere to create more opportunities to improve performance and increase passenger numbers.

He highlighted the airline’s Gold Coast service, saying its first three months had recorded the highest load factor for a newly launched Fiji Airways route in Australia.

“The service added about 53,000 seats a year to the airline’s network between Fiji and the Gold Coast.”

Mr Scurrah also said Fiji Airways was expanding its services to Hong Kong, increasing flights to four times a week from September 22 and to five times a week by early 2027.

He said the airline was also strengthening connectivity between Fiji and Canada through its Vancouver service.

item.title: Kiran: Drug crisis puts young girls at risk
item.description: AN emerging drug crisis is putting more young girls at risk of pregnancy, trafficking and exploitation, says Women Minister Sashi Kiran. Speaking at the launch of the Empower Pacific National Shelter for Domestic Violence in Lautoka on Friday, Ms Kiran said authorities were increasingly encountering children affected by drugs and other forms of exploitation.
item.content:encoded:
AN emerging drug crisis is putting more young girls at risk of pregnancy, trafficking and exploitation, says Women Minister Sashi Kiran.

Speaking at the launch of the Empower Pacific National Shelter for Domestic Violence in Lautoka on Friday, Ms Kiran said authorities were increasingly encountering children affected by drugs and other forms of exploitation.

She said a recent street sweep in Lautoka resulted in a 16-year-old girl who was pregnant and had been living on the streets “for some time” being taken into care.

“We have not been able to reintegrate her back into her family – she’s 16, about to deliver,” she said.

Ms Kiran said girls as young as 13, 14 and 15 were becoming pregnant in the Lautoka and Nadi areas and were also being drawn into trafficking.

“We have a new emerging crisis of sorts of what’s happened to our girls in relation to drugs.”

She said the situation highlighted the need for greater emphasis on parenting and community support.

“We are failing our children at the parenting and at the community level.”

She said the role of facilities such as the new shelter had expanded beyond addressing domestic violence.

“Five years ago, and 10 years ago, we were only talking about domestic violence. Now we have to think about a much bigger net.”

“Children are impacted because their parents are doing drugs or they have been pushed into drugs.”

She said some children were also being lured into employment at a young age, with jobs that appeared legal but had illegal activities behind them.

item.title: Plans for power expansion
item.description: FIJI’S electricity demand is growing by about five per cent a year, putting pressure on Energy Fiji Limited (EFL) to develop new generation capacity and strengthen the electricity grid. EFL chairman Rokoseru Nabalarua told the Fiji Australia Business Forum that the growth was a positive sign of economic activity and national development, but was also tightening the country’s reserve margin and inc
item.content:encoded:
FIJI’S electricity demand is growing by about five per cent a year, putting pressure on Energy Fiji Limited (EFL) to develop new generation capacity and strengthen the electricity grid.

EFL chairman Rokoseru Nabalarua told the Fiji Australia Business Forum that the growth was a positive sign of economic activity and national development, but was also tightening the country’s reserve margin and increasing the urgency for new power capacity.

“Fiji’s electricity system is currently in transition, with hydropower remaining the country’s main renewable source,” he said.

“Hydro generates slightly more than 615 gigawatt hours (GWh) a year, while fossil-fuel generation remains a significant part of the electricity mix.

“Independent power producers contribute about 86 GWh annually.”

Mr Nabalarua said EFL’s renewable targets, about 60 per cent by 2027 and 90 per cent by 2035, would require a significant expansion of renewable generation.

He said while hydropower would remain central, solar with storage, wind, biomass and other renewable sources would need to expand substantially.

However, he said fossil fuels would remain necessary during the transition to provide reliability while existing capacity was replaced, and the electricity grid was strengthened.

“The transition must therefore be orderly and engineered and financeable.”

He said EFL needed to ensure new generation, energy storage and grid capacity were developed ahead of demand so that constraints did not become visible to customers and investors.

item.title: Treatment payment | Court sides with family
item.description: A LEGAL argument that Fiji’s public hospitals cannot demand upfront payment from urgent or poor patients before providing necessary treatment has been accepted by the Supreme Court. Lawyer Niven Padarath advanced the argument while representing Rajesh Chandra, administrator of the estate of his late son, in proceedings against the permanent secretary for Health, Ministry of Health and attorney-gen
item.content:encoded:
A LEGAL argument that Fiji’s public hospitals cannot demand upfront payment from urgent or poor patients before providing necessary treatment has been accepted by the Supreme Court.

Lawyer Niven Padarath advanced the argument while representing Rajesh Chandra, administrator of the estate of his late son, in proceedings against the permanent secretary for Health, Ministry of Health and attorney-general.

At the heart of the case was a critical question: can a patient be admitted to a public hospital because their condition is urgent, but then effectively be denied the treatment they need because they cannot pay?

Mr Padarath argued that such an interpretation would undermine the protections contained in the Public Hospitals and Dispensaries Act.

His argument arose from the circumstances surrounding Mr Chandra’s son, who suffered from chronic kidney disease and needed short-term dialysis to keep him alive long enough to travel to India for further testing and treatment.

Justice Terence Arnold, in the August 28 Supreme Court ruling, recorded that Mr Padarath challenged the distinction drawn between admission and treatment.

“For the Petitioner, Mr Padarath argued that the Court of Appeal had over-emphasised the distinction between admission and continued treatment in its reasoning,” Justice Arnold said.

Mr Padarath submitted that the legislation was intended to ensure people admitted because of urgency or poverty could obtain not simply a hospital bed, but medical care and treatment.

His argument highlighted what he considered a fundamental inconsistency: a hospital could not demand money from an urgent or poor patient as a condition of admission, only to demand payment immediately afterwards before treating them.

The Supreme Court accepted his interpretation.

“I agree with the interpretation of the provisions advanced by Mr Padarath,” Justice Arnold said.

The significance of that finding extends beyond the individual circumstances of the case.

The court concluded that people admitted because of urgency or poverty cannot be required to make an upfront payment or provide a payment guarantee for treatment.

In Mr Chandra’s case, the court found short-term dialysis was available and would have prolonged his life sufficiently for him to travel to India.

He did not receive it because he could not afford to pay.

The Supreme Court allowed the appeal and sent the case back to the High Court for damages to be assessed.

item.title: Housing plan sparks backlash
item.description: CONCERNS are mounting that a proposed 61-lot gated residential development on part of Pacific Harbour’s historic golf course could place pressure on the community’s infrastructure and exceed the capacity envisaged in the area’s original masterplan. Residents gathered over the weekend to oppose the proposal by Speedy Heros Ltd, raising concerns over infrastructure capacity, the loss of part of an e
item.content:encoded:
CONCERNS are mounting that a proposed 61-lot gated residential development on part of Pacific Harbour’s historic golf course could place pressure on the community’s infrastructure and exceed the capacity envisaged in the area’s original masterplan.

Residents gathered over the weekend to oppose the proposal by Speedy Heros Ltd, raising concerns over infrastructure capacity, the loss of part of an established recreational asset, environmental impacts and what they say was a lack of meaningful community consultation.

Planning approval has been issued for the subdivision of Lot 2 DP 4114, River Drive, Pacific Harbour, into 61 residential lots, an open space reserve and an access road, subject to planning, engineering and environmental conditions.

Pacific Harbour resident Mark Sperling said residents were concerned they had only recently learned that approval had been granted.

“We’re very pleased we’ve had a good turnout,” Mr Sperling said. “The residents of Pacific Harbour that have just heard about it, obviously we are very upset about it.”

Mr Sperling said removing two holes from the golf course would reduce it from 18 holes to 16, potentially affecting its championship status.

Resident Viliame Takayawa said the golf course had significant sporting and historical value, having hosted international players including Greg Norman and Vijay Singh.

“There’s a lot of history attached to this golf course,” Mr Tawakaya said.

“It’s not about who plays and who’s staying around here. It’s the heritage.”

Submissions to planning authorities describe the golf course as a defining feature of Pacific Harbour for more than 50 years, contributing to tourism, property values, recreation and community identity.

Residents say they are not opposed to development, but want authorities to reconsider the approval, conduct further consultation and demonstrate that the project can be supported by existing infrastructure without undermining the viability of the remaining golf course.
